# Draft:King Tutankhamun's Reign over Egypt

King Tutankhamun’s Reign over Egypt
Introduction
King Tutankhamun, commonly known as King Tut, was a pharaoh of ancient Egypt’s Eighteenth Dynasty who ruled during the late 14th century BCE. Although his reign was brief and he was relatively insignificant politically during his lifetime, Tutankhamun holds immense historical importance today due to the extraordinary discovery of his intact tomb in 1922, which transformed modern understanding of ancient Egyptian culture and royal burial practices.
Historical Background
Tutankhamun ascended the throne around 1332 BCE, when he was approximately eight or nine years old. He was born during a period of political and religious instability caused by the reign of his probable father, Akhenaten. Akhenaten had radically transformed Egyptian religion by abandoning traditional polytheism in favor of worshiping a single deity, the Aten, disrupting centuries‑old religious traditions and weakening the power of the priesthood of Amun.
When Akhenaten died, Egypt was economically strained, diplomatically weakened, and internally divided. Tutankhamun inherited this unstable kingdom as a child ruler under the guidance of powerful advisers rather than as an autonomous monarch.
Sources:
Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Tutankhamun”
Oxford Encyclopedia of Ancient Egypt
Restoration of Traditional Religion
One of the most significant aspects of Tutankhamun’s reign was the restoration of traditional Egyptian religious practices. Early in his rule, he reversed Akhenaten’s monotheistic reforms and reinstated worship of the traditional gods, especially Amun, the chief deity of Thebes.
This religious shift is clearly documented in the Restoration Stela, a stone inscription issued during Tutankhamun’s reign. The decree describes how temples had fallen into ruin and ritual practices had ceased, and it proclaims the king’s role in repairing temples, reopening shrines, and reinstating priesthoods. He also changed his name from Tutankhaten (“Living image of the Aten”) to Tutankhamun (“Living image of Amun”), symbolizing the religious reversal.
Sources:
The Restoration Stela (Karnak)
British Museum, Ancient Egypt collection
Governance and Political Power
Because Tutankhamun was so young, actual political power was exercised by senior officials, primarily Ay, his vizier, and Horemheb, a leading general. These men likely directed state policy, military affairs, and foreign relations while the king served as the symbolic head of state.
During Tutankhamun’s reign, Egypt sought to stabilize its foreign territories, especially in Nubia and the Near East. Military campaigns may have been conducted under Horemheb’s authority, although inscriptions suggest limited success in restoring Egypt’s earlier imperial dominance.
Although Tutankhamun was not a strong independent ruler, his reign represented a return to political conservatism and stability, undoing many of the disruptions introduced by his predecessor.
Sources:
National Geographic, “Tutankhamun”
Redford, Akhenaten: The Heretic King
Death and Burial
Tutankhamun died around 1323 BCE, at roughly 18 or 19 years of age. The exact cause of his death remains unclear. Modern scientific studies, including CT scans and DNA analyses, suggest he suffered from multiple health issues, including malaria, a broken leg, and inherited conditions possibly linked to royal inbreeding.
Due to his sudden death, Tutankhamun was buried hastily in a relatively small tomb (KV62) in the Valley of the Kings. Unlike most royal tombs, his grave escaped extensive looting, allowing the preservation of over 5,000 artifacts, including the iconic gold funerary mask.
Sources:
Hawass et al., Ancestry and Pathology of King Tutankhamun
Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art
Historical Significance
While Tutankhamun achieved little as a ruling pharaoh, his legacy is profound. The discovery of his tomb by Howard Carter in 1922 provided unprecedented insight into royal funerary customs, craftsmanship, religious beliefs, and daily life in ancient Egypt. The artifacts reshaped global interest in Egyptology and remain among the most valuable archaeological finds in history.
Today, King Tut is remembered less for his reign and more for what his burial revealed about one of the world’s greatest ancient civilizations.
Sources:
Carter, The Tomb of Tut.Ankh.Amen
Metropolitan Museum of Art, Egyptian Art Collection
Conclusion
King Tutankhamun’s reign was short and largely dictated by advisers, yet it marked a crucial restoration period following one of Egypt’s most radical religious disruptions. Though he ruled quietly, his posthumous impact has been immense, making him one of the most recognizable figures in ancient history.
